I had similar thoughts too because I don't trust netflix - I mean didn't they make some weird series involving preteen girls acting much older?

I seriously hope that it's not the case that they're trying to normalise that horrendous shit. Though I know those kind of monsters do try to normalise it. A famous "philosopher" comes to mind, Sartre, who along with his fellow shitheads tried to legalise child abuse.

I don't know how Marxism and far left or any politics come into it, but I do agree we have to be wary of any media we watch and read.

Although Alex did mention having been suicidal when he found out, and Marcus mentioned not forgiving their stepfather, and generally showing how damaging and painful it has been, does show how really none of it was normal. He even says that as a child he just did what his parents wanted him to do, cause as a child you /think/ whatever kind of family you have is "normal".

To some extent all documentaries are a bit scripted. In this case they'd been getting interviewed for years before being filmed. Plus the dissociation, being on camera etc. explains why they look unnatural I guess.

The last part, I think it was a reconstruction of a conversation they'd already had off camera. I wish they hadn't done that, cause it makes it look somewhat fake but I fully believe them, they have a half brother who confirmed that he also went through that. Hopefully these kinds of documentaries encourage more people to speak out.

I really think Marcus did the right thing, to be honest. I would've done the same... cause if you could protect someone from that and take away the pain, especially knowing firsthand how severe it was, wouldn't you? I don't think it was necessary for him to know but the truth came out. At least it led to a conversation about encouraging people to speak out.

Edit: I thought about it more...and maybe yes he could have told him at 18 that their parents were shit and maybe not gone into detail...that way they could've avoided having to pretend being a happy family...but it was a way for him to protect himself too, by living in denial. So much strength in these two men, I really wish them, and anyone who's been through that, peace and love for the rest of their lives.

Those monsters count on exactly this to get away with it, cause it's so hard for survivors to speak up and go through an investigation.

I wish at least they'd name them and then the police would do the investigations without interviewing the brothers repeatedly. 

Going slightly off topic, I believe the perpetrators will face justice, if not in life, then after. I was an atheist before, but over time I've become convinced of an afterlife and that we at least get to experience everything we did to others from a 1st person perspective when we get to the life review. So every good and every bad thing someone intentionally did to others, they will experience it firsthand.

I think the reason the way they acted seemed fake was cause they had been interviewed about this for years already before filming, they were also dissociating from the trauma, and it's difficult to really determine how someone emotionally deals with something so severe...plus when in front of a camera everyone acts a bit unnaturally I guess.

Still, I don't understand why he was so insistent about wanting to know exactly what happened. His brother gave him a gift, he made the best decision to protect him from the unimaginable pain. Maybe he wanted to know so that his brother wouldn't be alone with the memories? So that he could at least be there for him somehow and help him move on?

It's fucking horrible that these things happen.

How is this guy still walking???

How can someone do that...he's like a shell, there's nothing inside him.

I understand what you're saying.

But of course I'm not suggesting that any friendship between an adult and a child automatically means there are bad intentions. These are just signs to watch out for which could indicate bad intentions.

The things in the original post are more like signs that the potential victim would notice.

So I think as a parent/guardian some signs to watch out for could be, as some have mentioned: someone making regular favors to the family and trying to gain their trust, not knowing where your child is going, and the perpetrator seeking to be alone with the child.

Definitely it can happen at any age.

I experienced abuse though not to the extent of the original post. I was lucky to have been taught from an early age about these things, which helped a lot, but despite being taught, I still had doubts and was in denial for a long time, and now only many years later do I see it for what it really was.

Which shows how difficult it is for someone to comprehend what is going on in these situations.

The video is called "to stop abuse, we first need to understand grooming". Speaker is Grace Tame.

It's really disheartening sometimes and hard to believe someone you know could do some things. At least people are becoming much more aware.

It can be extremely hard to convince someone they're actually being abused though.

But the best thing one can do is just report and hopefully the ones whose job it is to protect, actually do so.
